subject: chem
title: Halogenoalkanes
subtitle: Nucleophilic substitution, elimination, reactivity trends.
concept: Halogenoalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution because the C–X bond is polar (Cδ+–Xδ−) making carbon susceptible to nucleophilic attack.
Reactivity increases down Group 17 (C–I bonds break most easily) despite C–F being the most polar.
Elimination competes with substitution; high temperature and concentrated base (ethanolic KOH) favour elimination.

notes.heading: Structure and Polarity
items: Halogenoalkanes (haloalkanes) contain a C–X bond (X = F, Cl, Br or I). The electronegativity of the halogen makes the carbon δ+ — susceptible to attack by nucleophiles. Reactivity in nucleophilic substitution: C–I > C–Br > C–Cl > C–F. Despite C–F being the most polar bond, bond enthalpy dominates — C–F is very strong (485 kJ mol⁻¹) and barely reacts.

notes.heading: Nucleophilic Substitution
items: With warm aqueous NaOH: RX + OH⁻ → ROH + X⁻ (substitution → alcohol).
With KCN in ethanol: RX + CN⁻ → RCN + X⁻ (substitution → nitrile; chain length increases by 1 carbon).
With excess NH₃ in a sealed tube: RX + NH₃ → RNH₂ + HX (substitution → primary amine).

AgNO₃ test for halide ions (after acid hydrolysis): Cl⁻ → white AgCl (dissolves in dilute NH₃); Br⁻ → cream AgBr (dissolves in concentrated NH₃); I⁻ → yellow AgI (insoluble in NH₃). Rate of precipitation: I > Br > Cl (reflects C–X bond strength).

notes.heading: Elimination
items: Hot ethanolic KOH (or NaOH) causes elimination — HX is removed to form an alkene. The competition between substitution and elimination depends on conditions: aqueous/warm → substitution; ethanolic/hot → elimination.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes favour elimination (steric hindrance around the C–X carbon prevents nucleophilic attack).

notes.heading: CFCs and the Environment
items: CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) are very stable in the troposphere but diffuse to the stratosphere. UV radiation cleaves the C–Cl bond homolytically, generating Cl• radicals. Each Cl• can catalyse the destruction of thousands of O₃ molecules: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; ClO• + O• → Cl• + O₂. The Cl• is regenerated — catalytic cycle.
HCFCs and HFCs were introduced as replacements — they contain C–H bonds that react with OH• radicals in the troposphere before reaching the stratosphere.

definitions.body: A reaction in which a nucleophile replaces an atom or group (usually a halide leaving group) at a carbon atom.
An atom or group that departs with its bonding electrons during a substitution reaction; halide ions are good leaving groups.
A reaction in which a small molecule (e.g. HX) is removed from an organic molecule to form a double bond.

workedExamples.q: Predict and explain whether 1-bromopropane or 1-iodopropane undergoes nucleophilic substitution more rapidly with NaOH(aq).

steps.text: C–I bond enthalpy (~238 kJ mol⁻¹) < C–Br bond enthalpy (~290 kJ mol⁻¹).
The C–X bond must break in the rate-determining step. A weaker bond is easier to break.
1-Iodopropane reacts faster because the C–I bond is weaker and breaks more easily, even though C–I is less polar than C–Br.

mistakes: Saying C–F is most reactive because it is most polar — C–F is so strong it barely reacts; bond enthalpy dominates over polarity for reactivity.
Using aqueous KOH for elimination — it must be ethanolic KOH (hot) to favour elimination.
Forgetting that nucleophilic substitution with NaCN increases the carbon chain length by 1.
tips: Silver nitrate test after hydrolysis: warm with AgNO₃(aq): Cl → white AgCl; Br → cream AgBr; I → yellow AgI. Add NH₃: AgCl dissolves in dilute; AgBr only in concentrated; AgI insoluble in both.
Conditions summary: NaOH(aq) warm → substitution (alcohol); KOH ethanolic hot → elimination (alkene); NH₃ excess sealed → amine; NaCN ethanol → nitrile.

flashcards.q: Why does C–I react faster in nucleophilic substitution than C–F, despite C–F being more polar?
flashcards.a: Bond enthalpy is more important than polarity — C–I is much weaker than C–F, so the rate-determining step (C–X bond breaking) is faster for C–I.

flashcards.q: What product forms when a halogenoalkane reacts with NaCN in ethanol?
flashcards.a: A nitrile (R–CN); the carbon chain length increases by one carbon atom.

flashcards.q: What conditions favour elimination over substitution in halogenoalkanes?
flashcards.a: Hot, concentrated ethanolic KOH (vs warm aqueous NaOH for substitution).

flashcards.q: Describe the AgNO₃ test for halide ions.
flashcards.a: Add AgNO₃(aq) after hydrolysis: Cl⁻ → white AgCl; Br⁻ → cream AgBr; I⁻ → yellow AgI. Test with NH₃ to confirm: AgCl dissolves in dilute NH₃; AgBr in concentrated; AgI is insoluble in both.

flashcards.q: Why do CFCs cause ozone depletion?
flashcards.a: In the stratosphere, UV breaks C–Cl bonds → Cl• radicals. Cl• catalyses: O₃ → O₂ (each Cl• can destroy thousands of O₃ molecules).

flashcards.q: What is formed when a halogenoalkane reacts with excess NH₃?

questions.q: Which product forms when 1-bromobutane reacts with warm aqueous NaOH?
questions.exp: Warm aqueous NaOH = nucleophilic substitution: R–Br + OH⁻ → R–OH (butan-1-ol) + Br⁻.

questions.q: Which halogenoalkane reacts fastest in nucleophilic substitution?
questions.exp: C–I has the lowest bond enthalpy → breaks most easily → fastest nucleophilic substitution.

questions.q: What is the observation when AgNO₃(aq) is added to a hydrolysed sample of 1-chloroethane?
questions.exp: Cl⁻ ions give a white AgCl precipitate with Ag⁺.

questions.q: Which conditions give an alkene from a halogenoalkane?
questions.exp: Ethanolic KOH (hot) favours elimination → HX removed → alkene formed.

questions.q: What is produced when CH₃CH₂Br reacts with NaCN in ethanol?
questions.exp: NaCN substitutes CN⁻ for Br⁻: CH₃CH₂Br + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CN (propanenitrile) + Br⁻. Chain length increases by 1C.
